newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Western analysts await steps by Romanian reformers.
newsitem.headline: Western analysts await steps by Romanian reformers.

text.p: Foreign analysts on Wednesday welcomed the reformist opposition's victory in Romania's election but reserved final judgment pending news of a detailed programme and the outcome of the November 17 presidential race.
"It's relatively positive, it looks positive as pro-reform parties won the election," Merrill Lynch senior economist Andrew Kenningham said by telephone from London.
The opposition Democratic Convention (CDR) scored about 30 percent in Sunday's parliamentary polls and is holding talks with two other parties to form a government and share out key portfolios.
Incumbent Ion Iliescu led the opening round of the presidential contest and faces a run-off against CDR leader Emil Constantinescu.

A win by Constantinescu would leave a new coalition free to pursue its programme unhindered. But Iliescu denies accusations that his slow reforms have caused mass poverty and says he will be a stabilising factor in any fight with a hostile government.
"It's important to wait until we know the outcome of the presidential elections, see the overall balance of power between the president and parliament," said analyst Marc Holdsworth from ING Barings.
"I think the opposition made all the right noises, they look more qualified...even more committed to the integration with Western Europe and NATO."
The CDR offered voters a "Contract with Romania" with plenty of promises -- tax cuts, increased pensions, soft loans for housing and upgrading backward rural infrastructure.
But anaylsts said they needed evidence that a new government would draw up tough monetary and fiscal policies to address the economy's problems.
"Attitudes to Romania could change but policies have to be implemented," said one London-based banker. "I think it will be three to six months before things really start getting done."

Economists say the outgoing government has bequeathed several headaches, including annual inflation of 45 percent, a currency artificially propped on interbank markets and bulging trade and budget deficits.
They say Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu's cabinet has delayed the restructuring of communist-era industry and limited unemployment by keeping afloat inefficient state companies.
"It is very clear that what is needed is a macroeconomic stabilisation and a structural programme," Kenningham said.
"We haven't seen a very detailed economic programme. A lot of things which will have to be done are going to be tough policies, some people losing jobs."
The analysts said austerity programmes were compounded by the coming winter, despite assurances by the current government that there will be no repeat of the 1995 energy crunch.

A new administration will have to improve ties with the International Monetary Fund, which suspended credits earlier this year. It also must find a trade-off between sound economics and limiting social costs to impoverished consumers.

"Foreign investors' concern is that urgent action should be taken but stability maintained," Holdsworth said. "The concern is that Romania would become like Bulgaria rather than going the way of more succesful states such as Hungary and Poland.
